scenario_constructions: Priya Chandrasekaran and this specific assemblage are fictional, invented for this case -- consistent with corpus convention (e.g. Rosa Delgado / Fermenter, Dana Osei / The Cold Hit). The R7-2 zoning designation, its real FAR/yard/plaza rules, and the real Broadway-diagonal-block phenomenon are real and cited directly by name.

The three 'as-is' parcels' exact vertex coordinates, areas (11,000 / 7,900 / 11,100 sq ft), and the consolidated lot's dimensions (200 ft x 150 ft) are a constructed scenario, mathematically self-consistent (verified: the three parcel areas sum exactly to the consolidated lot's 30,000 sq ft, and shared cut-line edge lengths match between adjoining parcels) but not derived from any one real, specific surveyed address.

The regular octagon plaza's side length (30 ft) and apothem (36.2 ft) are constructed scenario dimensions, chosen so the plaza's real-formula-computed area clears the cited real minimum (S4) with room to spare.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: The simplified yard rule: every non-front lot line requires the yard, and a concave parcel's notch lot lines are also treated as requiring it
modeling_assumptions.basis: Real zoning lot-line classification for irregular, multi-frontage parcels is materially more detailed than this case models -- disclosed as a simplification so the arithmetic is tractable at this grade band.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Affects both options in the same direction (irregular shapes lose more), so it is not the main driver of which option wins.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Lead time to start of construction for each option
modeling_assumptions.basis: No public source publishes standard permit-review or lot-merger-filing timelines for a specific city; set to reflect that a lot-line merger genuinely requires additional real process (owner agreements, a replat filing) beyond standard permit review.
No single universal planning horizon exists across cities; many long-range housing plans use multi-year horizons in this general range. Set as a disclosed scenario dial.

sensitivity_note: No SPEC Section 6 subject-matter sensitivity applies. This is a zoning/housing-capacity planning decision with no death, illness, or family-hardship stakes.

balance.argument_a: Plat As-Is wins if the planning horizon is short enough that Option B's extra 12 months of lead time erases more housing-supply value than its larger eventual unit count adds back -- and a real, disclosed scenario (the twist) shows that threshold is not hypothetical: a housing-production deadline moved up from 10 years to 5 years flips the winner outright, because B's units simply don't have as many years left in the (now shorter) window to count.
balance.argument_b: Replat & Consolidate wins on the city's stated 10-year planning horizon (5.89% margin) because a single larger, regular zoning lot loses proportionally less area to the required yard than three small irregular parcels do -- especially the concave one -- so it realizes about 18% more buildable footprint and, at the same FAR, meaningfully more total dwelling units; over a long enough horizon that extra density outweighs the 12-month process delay.
balance.margin_basis: Compute buildable footprint for each option from Appendix C/D's parcel geometry and Appendix B's required yard depth, convert to dwelling units via Appendix B's FAR and Appendix E's average unit size, then compute dwelling-unit-years delivered within Appendix E's stated planning horizon, net of each option's lead time.
balance.twist_effect: The city's housing-production planning horizon is shortened from 10 years to 5 years (a real, plausible policy dynamic -- an accelerated mayoral housing deadline). Two Tier 2 P4 adversarial passes (2026-09-18) each found a real, student-exploitable unstated convention and both are now explicitly foreclosed in the twist narration itself (FACILITATOR.md and the Interactive HTML): (1) the twist applies to every project not yet under construction, with no grandfathering for a zoning lot merger already mid-filing -- closing off a real-world vested-rights objection that could otherwise exempt Option B; and (2) 'mid-filing' does NOT entitle Option B to any partial credit for lead time already spent -- sensitivity_model.py's evaluate_twist() always charges the full stated lead_B (18 months) against the shortened horizon, and the twist now says so explicitly, because a natural reading of 'already mid-filing' as '~half done, so only ~9 months should still count' mathematically reverses the intended winner flip (B would win again, 491.4 vs 439.7 unit-years, if given ~9 months of credit). This penalizes Option B's longer 18-month lead time much more heavily than Option A's 6-month lead time, because fewer of B's years of eventual delivery now fall within the shorter window. Post-twist: A = 439.68 unit-years, B = 404.71 unit-years, an 8.64% margin, winner flips to Plat As-Is (A). Disclosed here and in sensitivity_model.py; never in case.md or FACILITATOR.md's student-facing sections.
balance.stability: Base margin (5.89%) is a direct, computable function of the three disclosed Modeling Assumption dials (MA3's two lead times, MA4's horizon) via sensitivity_model.py. Per sensitivity_disclosure[], lead_B and horizon each flip the winner at a +/-50% flex; lead_A does not. No flex breaches the SPEC Section 2 20% cap in either direction -- a comparatively stable case relative to its sibling (The Cold Hit), disclosed honestly either way.

sensitivity_disclosure.justification: MA3 has no citable timeline source. Flexing +50% (to 9 months) narrows B's win to 3.17%, still within cap; flexing -50% (to 3 months) widens B's win to 8.75%, still within cap. Does not flip the winner in either direction -- the least load-bearing of the three dials.

MA3, no citable timeline source. Flexing +50% (to 27 months) flips the winner to A (3.58%, within cap); flexing -50% (to 9 months) widens B's win to 15.23%, still within cap. One of the two most load-bearing assumptions.

MA4, a disclosed scenario dial with no single universal real value. Flexing +50% (to 15 years) widens B's win to 10.18%, within cap; flexing -50% (to 5 years) flips the winner to A (8.64%, within cap) -- this is also exactly the lever the twist pulls, deliberately, so a facilitator can connect the twist directly back to this disclosure.

deliverables.text: A parcel classification table (Polygon, Irregular Polygon, Convex, Concave) for the three 'as-is' parcels, identifying which is concave and where its notch is, plus a missing-interior-angle calculation for Parcel L1 using the sum-of-interior-angles theorem.
A buildable-footprint table for Option A (Plat As-Is): required-yard area and buildable footprint per parcel, and the combined buildable-footprint percentage.
A buildable-footprint calculation for Option B's consolidated lot, plus the area of the regular octagon plaza (using the regular-polygon area formula) checked against the real minimum plaza size.
A dwelling-unit-years comparison between Option A and Option B, using FAR, average unit size, lead times, and the planning horizon, with the percent margin.
A short written reflection using the term Population on why cities end up with blocks shaped like this one, and whether Priya's simplified yard rule is reasonable.
